title: Electric Generators
lead: Turn the shaft of a motor by hand and the machine runs the other way, turning motion into an emf: it becomes an electric generator. This section finds the average and the instantaneous emf of a coil turning in a magnetic field, and the way slip rings or a split ring hand that emf on to a circuit.
objectives: Calculate the emf induced in a generator.
Calculate the peak emf which can be induced in a particular generator system.
summary_html:
• An electric generator rotates a coil in a magnetic field, inducing an emfgiven as a function of time by $\kemf = NA\kBmag\kw\sin\kw\kt ,$ where $A$ is the area of an $N$-turn coil rotated at a constant angular velocity $\kw$ in a uniform magnetic field $\kBmag$.
  • The peak emf $\kemfo$ of a generator is $\kemfo = NA\kBmag\kw .$

Nothing else in the module is left out. All four of its drawings are redrawn as one turning generator with the book’s own images beside it, since the book draws one machine four times, and the steam turbine is kept as a photograph, because the passage it sits under is about it. (Figure 23.20) A generator with a single rectangular coil rotated at constant angular velocity in a uniform magnetic field produces an emf that varies sinusoidally in time. Note the generator is similar to a motor, except the shaft is rotated to produce a current rather than the other way around. (Figure 23.21) The emf of a generator is sent to a light bulb with the system of rings and brushes shown. The graph gives the emf of the generator as a function of time. emf₀ is the peak emf. exercises.prompt: Using RHR-1, show that the emfs in the sides of the generator loop in Figure 23.22 are in the same sense and thus add.

answer.solution: The two side wires move in opposite directions, so RHR-1 gives forces on their charges that are opposite in space, up one side and down the other, and that is the same sense around the loop. Take the field pointing from the north pole on the left to the south pole on the right, the shaft vertical, and the loop turning counterclockwise seen from above. At the instant the plane of the loop lies along the field, the left side wire moves toward you and the right side wire moves away, because the two sides sit on opposite sides of the shaft. For the left wire, point the thumb of the right hand along $\kv$, toward you, and the fingers along $\kBmag$, to the right; the palm faces up, so the force on a positive charge pushes it up the wire. For the right wire $\kv$ points away from you with the same field, and the force is down the wire. A charge pushed up the left side, across the top, down the right side and back across the bottom goes around the loop one way, so both emfs drive current in the same sense. Each side contributes $\kBmag\ell\kv\sin\ktheta$, and they add to $\kemf = 2\kBmag\ell\kv\sin\ktheta$. At any other angle both velocities turn together and keep opposite directions, so the emfs still add.

exercises.prompt: The source of a generator’s electrical energy output is the work done to turn its coils. How is the work needed to turn the generator related to Lenz’s law?

answer.solution: Lenz's law says that the current induced in the coil opposes the change in flux that produced it. That current flows in the coil while the coil sits in the magnetic field, so the field exerts a force on it, and its direction is exactly the one whose force opposes the motion of the coil. The generator therefore resists turning. The faster you turn it, or the more current it must supply, the harder it pushes back. Whoever turns the shaft does work against that opposing torque, and that work is the source of the electrical energy the generator delivers. If Lenz's law ran the other way, the induced current would help the coil round, and the generator would spin itself faster and faster and deliver energy out of nothing. Lenz's law is conservation of energy written for induction. It is also why a bicycle generator is easy to turn with its lamp off and hard to turn with the lamp on. With no current there is no opposing force and no work; with a current, the work done against the opposing force lights the lamp.

exercises.prompt: The emf induced in a coil that is rotating in a magnetic field will be at a maximum when

options: the magnetic flux is at a maximum.
the magnetic flux is at a minimum.
the change in magnetic flux is at a maximum.
the change in magnetic flux is at a minimum.
answer.hint: Faraday's law makes the emf the rate at which the flux changes, not the flux itself. Ask where on a cosine the value is changing fastest, and notice that it is where the value itself is passing through zero.

exercises.prompt: A coil with circular cross section and 20 turns is rotating at a rate of 400 rpm between the poles of a magnet. If the magnetic field strength is 0.6 T and peak voltage is 0.2 V, what is the radius of the coil? If the emf of the coil is zero at $\kt = 0\;\text{s}$, when will it reach its peak emf?

answer.solution: The radius is $1.1\;\text{cm}$, and the emf first reaches its peak at $\kt = 0.0375\;\text{s}$. The peak emf is $\kemfo = N\karea\kBmag\kw$. The rotation rate in radians per second is $\kw = (400\;\text{rev/min})(2\pi\;\text{rad/rev})/(60\;\text{s/min}) = 41.9\;\text{rad/s}$. Solving for the area, $\karea = \kemfo/N\kBmag\kw = (0.2\;\text{V})/[(20)(0.6\;\text{T})(41.9\;\text{rad/s})] = 3.98\times 10^{-4}\;\text{m}^2$. The cross section is circular, so $\karea = \pi r^2$ and $r = \sqrt{(3.98\times 10^{-4}\;\text{m}^2)/\pi} = 1.13\times 10^{-2}\;\text{m}$, about 1.1 cm. Since the emf is zero at $\kt = 0$, it follows $\kemf = \kemfo\sin\kw\kt$, which first peaks when $\kw\kt = \pi/2$. Then $\kt = \pi/2\kw = (1.571\;\text{rad})/(41.9\;\text{rad/s}) = 0.0375\;\text{s}$. This is one quarter of the period $\kT = 2\pi/\kw = 0.150\;\text{s}$, the quarter turn that takes the coil from facing the field to standing edge-on to it.

exercises.prompt: Calculate the peak voltage of a generator that rotates its 200-turn, 0.100 m diameter coil at 3600 rpm in a 0.800 T field.

answer.hint: Use $\kemfo = NA\kBmag\kw$. The coil is circular of 0.100 m diameter, so its area is $\pi r^2$ with $r = 0.0500\;\text{m}$, and 3600 rpm must first be turned into radians per second.

exercises.prompt: What is the peak emf generated by rotating a 1000-turn, 20.0 cm diameter coil in the Earth’s $5\text{.}\text{00}\times {\text{10}}^{-5}\;\text{T}$ magnetic field, given the plane of the coil is originally perpendicular to the Earth’s field and is rotated to be parallel to the field in 10.0 ms?

answer.hint: The coil turns through a quarter revolution in 10.0 ms, so the angular velocity is $(\pi/2)$ radians divided by that time; then use $\kemfo = NA\kBmag\kw$ with the area of a circle of 10.0 cm radius.

exercises.prompt: (a) A bicycle generator rotates at 1875 rad/s, producing an 18.0 V peak emf. It has a 1.00 by 3.00 cm rectangular coil in a 0.640 T field. How many turns are in the coil? (b) Is this number of turns of wire practical for a 1.00 by 3.00 cm coil?

answer.hint: Solve $\kemfo = NA\kBmag\kw$ for $N$, taking the area as the product of the two sides of the rectangle in meters.

exercises.prompt: (a) A car generator turns at 400 rpm when the engine is idling. Its 300-turn, 5.00 by 8.00 cm rectangular coil rotates in an adjustable magnetic field so that it can produce sufficient voltage even at low rpms. What is the field strength needed to produce a 24.0 V peak emf? (b) Discuss how this required field strength compares to those available in permanent and electromagnets.

answer.hint: Solve $\kemfo = NA\kBmag\kw$ for the field strength, turning 400 rpm into radians per second first and taking the area as 5.00 cm by 8.00 cm in meters.
answer.solution:
(a) 0.477 T
(b) This field strength is small enough that it can be obtained using either a permanent magnet or an electromagnet.

exercises.prompt: A 75-turn, 10.0 cm diameter coil rotates at an angular velocity of 8.00 rad/s in a 1.25 T field, starting with the plane of the coil parallel to the field. (a) What is the peak emf? (b) At what time is the peak emf first reached? (c) At what time is the emf first at its most negative? (d) What is the period of the AC voltage output?

parts.hint: Use $\kemfo = NA\kBmag\kw$ with the area of a circle of 5.00 cm radius.
The coil starts with its plane along the field, which is the edge-on position where the emf is already at its peak, so no time has to pass at all.
The emf is at its most negative half a period after it is at its peak, and the period is $2\pi/\kw$.
The period of the output is $\kT = 2\pi/\kw$.

exercises.prompt: **Unreasonable Results** A 500-turn coil with a $0\text{.}\text{250}\;{\text{m}}^{2}$ area is spun in the Earth’s $5\text{.}\text{00}\times {\text{10}}^{-5}\;\text{T}$ field, producing a 12.0 kV maximum emf. (a) At what angular velocity must the coil be spun? (b) What is unreasonable about this result? (c) Which assumption or premise is responsible?

answer.hint: Solve $\kemfo = NA\kBmag\kw$ for the angular velocity, and keep the field in teslas and the emf in volts.
answer.solution:
(a) $1\text{.}\text{92}\times {\text{10}}^{6}\;\text{rad/s}$
(b) This angular velocity is unreasonably high, higher than can be obtained for any mechanical system.
(c) The assumption that a voltage as great as 12.0 kV could be obtained is unreasonable.

derivations.what: the emf of a generator coil

assumes.text: The velocity of each side wire is at an angle $\ktheta$ with $\kBmag$, so its component perpendicular to $\kBmag$ is $\kv\sin\ktheta$.
The emfs induced on the two side wires are in the same direction; the top and bottom segments add none.
The coil rotates at a constant angular velocity $\kw$.
A coil of $N$ loops has $N$ times the emf of one loop.

then.why: The motional emf, with $\kv$ perpendicular to $\kBmag$.
